pctRange: varies (extract — often listed high, e.g. 70–96% snail secretion filtrate)
ceilingNote: A high % mainly signals more humectant feel; beyond a point it adds tackiness, not benefit.
plainRead: On a Korean label a big snail % (e.g. 96%) is a marketing/feel cue, not a standardized active dose — there's no agreed effective concentration, so treat it as a hydrating base.

pctRange: varies (extract; standardized formulas often cited around 0.1–1% of actives)
ceilingNote: More extract isn't linearly better; the soothing comes from specific triterpenes, not raw percentage.
plainRead: A centella/cica % on the label rarely tells you the active triterpene content — look instead for standardized actives like madecassoside if you want a measurable dose.

ceilingNote: Above ~5–10% offers little extra and more often triggers flushing or irritation in sensitive skin.
plainRead: A label listing 2–5% niacinamide is in the well-supported sweet spot; a '10%' product is not twice as good and may simply read as more irritating.

pctRange: 0.1–2% (as raw HA; finished serums often ~1–2%)
ceilingNote: Past ~2% it gets sticky/tacky and can feel drying in low humidity — more isn't more hydration.
plainRead: HA percentages look tiny because a little goes a long way; a '2% HA complex' is already high — apply to damp skin and seal to see the benefit.

pctRange: ~0.1–1% (ceramide content; full lipid blends higher)
ceilingNote: Balance with cholesterol/fatty acids matters more than raw ceramide %; excess alone doesn't help.
plainRead: You'll rarely see a meaningful ceramide % on the label; what matters is the lipid ratio in the formula, not a single headline number.

ceilingNote: Above ~5% adds little and can feel slightly tacky; it's a supporting soother, not a dose-chasing active.
plainRead: 1–5% panthenol on a label is plenty; it's a gentle hydrator/soother where higher numbers don't translate to visibly better results.

pctRange: varies (extract — ampoules often listed 10–80%+ propolis extract)
ceilingNote: A high listed % is a feel/marketing cue, not a standardized active dose; allergy risk (bee products) is the real ceiling.
plainRead: A big propolis % on a Korean ampoule signals a richer, glow-giving base — not a measured active strength; patch test if you react to bee products.

pctRange: varies (extract; essences often listed very high, e.g. 90%+)
ceilingNote: A high mugwort % reflects a watery extract base, not concentrated potency; more doesn't mean stronger calming.
plainRead: '100% mugwort' style claims mean the water phase is mugwort extract, not that it's a high-strength active — read it as a gentle soothing base.

pctRange: varies (extract; toners often listed up to ~70–90%+)
ceilingNote: High listed % is a base-feel cue; standardized heartleaf actives aren't established, so percentage ≠ potency.
plainRead: A heartleaf/Houttuynia toner boasting a high % is mostly a diluted botanical water — a soothing base, not a dose you can compare to acids or niacinamide.

pctRange: varies (extract/ferment; often listed high in essences)
ceilingNote: A high rice % signals a nourishing essence base, not a standardized brightening dose.
plainRead: Rice extract percentages on K-beauty labels are about the 'glow/mochi' feel of the base, not a measurable active level — there's no consensus effective %.

pctRange: varies (extract; luxury serums often listed high, no standard active %)
ceilingNote: Saponin (ginsenoside) content matters more than raw extract %, which is rarely disclosed.
plainRead: A high ginseng % on a hanbang label is a premium positioning cue; it doesn't tell you the ginsenoside dose that actually drives the antioxidant glow.

pctRange: varies (extract; serums commonly ~1–5% extract, essences higher)
ceilingNote: Polyphenol (EGCG) content and stability matter more than headline extract %.
plainRead: A green-tea % tells you little about active polyphenols; freshness and formulation (dark packaging) matter more than the number on the label.

pctRange: varies (ferment filtrate — first-essences often listed 90–95%+)
ceilingNote: A 90%+ listing is the essence base itself, not a concentrated active dose; more isn't proportionally brighter.
plainRead: '95% galactomyces' means the essence is mostly ferment filtrate — read it as the product format, not a high-strength standardized active.

pctRange: varies (no established topical %; often ~0.5–2% sodium DNA in serums)
ceilingNote: Topical evidence is early; a higher % doesn't equal injectable-grade results and may just add cost.
plainRead: PDRN/'salmon DNA' percentages aren't standardized for topicals — treat any number as a cosmetic feel claim, not a clinical dose.

pctRange: varies (typically fractions of a % active; blends often 2–10% of a peptide solution)
ceilingNote: Peptides work at low signal-level concentrations; a big '10%' is usually the diluted trade-solution, not pure peptide.
plainRead: A '10% peptide complex' on a label is mostly the carrier solution — peptides act at tiny concentrations, so the headline % overstates the actual active.

pctRange: 10–20% (L-ascorbic acid); derivatives vary 1–10%
ceilingNote: Above ~20% L-ascorbic acid raises irritation with little added benefit and oxidizes faster.
plainRead: For pure vitamin C, 10–20% at low pH is the effective window; a gentler '5% derivative' is a different, milder molecule — don't compare the numbers directly.

ceilingNote: Above ~1% irritation rises sharply with limited extra benefit; build up slowly.
plainRead: 0.1–1% is the meaningful retinol range; a '1%' product is strong, not beginner-friendly — start low and increase frequency before strength.

ceilingNote: Most studies use ~0.5–1%; going higher hasn't shown added benefit.
plainRead: 0.5–2% bakuchiol is the typical studied range; it's gentler than retinol, but pregnancy-safety data is limited, so don't assume it's automatically pregnancy-safe.

pctRange: 5–10% (glycolic OTC); lactic up to ~10%
ceilingNote: Above ~10% (or pH below ~3) sharply increases stinging and barrier stress for home use.
plainRead: A 5–10% glycolic/lactic at pH 3–4 is the effective OTC zone; a high % at very low pH is a professional-style peel, not daily care.

ceilingNote: 2% is the practical OTC ceiling; higher mainly increases dryness and irritation, not pore-clearing.
plainRead: 0.5–2% salicylic acid is the standard range; '2%' is already the strong end for leave-on, so more isn't better for blackheads.

pctRange: 4–10% (gluconolactone/lactobionic)
ceilingNote: Larger molecules are gentler, so even higher % stays mild — but irritation can still creep up past ~10%.
plainRead: PHA percentages run higher than AHA/BHA because the molecule is bigger and milder; a '10% PHA' is gentler than a '10% glycolic,' so don't read the numbers as equivalent.

pctRange: 10% (OTC cosmetic); 15–20% is prescription-tier
ceilingNote: OTC tops out near 10%; higher strengths are regulated/medical, not standard cosmetics.
plainRead: A 10% azelaic product is the cosmetic OTC standard; '20%' figures refer to prescription products, so a higher label number usually means a different regulatory category.

ceilingNote: Above ~5% topically shows little added benefit; often paired with niacinamide rather than pushed higher.
plainRead: 2–5% tranexamic acid is the usual effective window for tone; a higher % isn't a proven upgrade, so pairing beats dose-chasing.

pctRange: 2% (alpha-arbutin)
ceilingNote: ~2% is the established sweet spot; higher can risk irritation/paradoxical effects with little gain.
plainRead: Around 2% alpha-arbutin is the recognized effective dose; a label boasting much more isn't a proven advantage and may just irritate.

pctRange: ~0.1–1% (purified active)
ceilingNote: It's effective at low purified percentages; very high figures are uncommon and not needed.
plainRead: Madecassoside is the standardized active from centella, so even a small % (0.1–1%) is meaningful — unlike a vague 'centella extract' number, this one is measurable.

pctRange: varies (typically ~0.1–0.5% active; some essences much higher base %)
ceilingNote: Effective at low active levels; a high listed % is often the diluted solution, not pure beta-glucan.
plainRead: Beta-glucan works at very low concentrations, so a small active % is fine; a big headline number usually reflects a watery base, not extra potency.

pctRange: varies (emollient; can be 1–100% in face oils)
ceilingNote: It's an emollient, not a dose-dependent active — '100% squalane' just means a pure oil, not a stronger treatment.
plainRead: Squalane % is about texture/richness, not active strength; pH doesn't apply to an oil, and 100% simply means an undiluted facial oil.
